subject: Banking
title: Proprietary Trading
description: A quick win: understand Proprietary Trading.

hook.text: Before 2010, investment banks traded billions of their own money in markets.

buildup.text: Proprietary trading means the bank bets its own capital on stocks, bonds, currencies, and derivatives for profit.

discovery.text: Prop traders used the bank's cheap funding and market information to gain an edge over regular investors.

twist.text: The Volcker Rule in 2010 banned most prop trading at banks. The risk was too high.

climax.text: Prop trading was the most profitable and dangerous activity in banking. Regulation killed it to protect the system.

punchline.text: $10 billion from trading. Too profitable and too dangerous. Now banned.

quiz.question: What did the Volcker Rule do?
options: Banned most proprietary trading at banks to reduce systemic risk

details.summary: Proprietary trading occurs when banks trade stocks, bonds, currencies, and derivatives using their own money rather than client funds, aiming to profit directly from market movements using specialized strategies and algorithms.
details.whyItMatters: Proprietary trading was once hugely profitable for banks but also created massive risk. The Volcker Rule restricted it after 2008 because banks were gambling with depositor-backed funds and taxpayer-guaranteed safety nets.
takeaways: Banks traded their own capital for profit, not on behalf of clients
The Volcker Rule of 2010 restricted proprietary trading at banks
Many prop traders left banks to join or start hedge funds

faq.question: Why was proprietary trading banned at banks?
faq.answer: Banks used depositor funds and government-guaranteed backstops to make risky bets. When those bets went wrong in 2008, taxpayers paid for the bailouts. The Volcker Rule aimed to separate risk-taking from government-insured banking.

faq.question: Did the Volcker Rule actually stop proprietary trading?
faq.answer: It reduced but did not eliminate it. Banks reclassified some prop trading as market making or hedging, which remain permitted. The line between allowed and prohibited trading is blurry and enforcement is challenging.
